decks.title: Waste Management — Part 1: Impact of waste and key environmental terms
goals: Explain three harmful effects of accumulated waste with local examples
Explain why waste management is essential in growing Indian cities
Define global warming, acid rain, eutrophication, biomagnification and thermal pollution, with one cause and one effect of each

slides.heading: Where does it all go?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Every home, market, factory and hospital produces **waste**. When it piles up uncollected or is dumped carelessly, it spoils the landscape, pollutes air, water and soil, and spreads disease. Waste also links to wider problems such as global warming and polluted lakes.

rows: Food scraps, paper, plastic, glass, old batteries

visual.alt: Table of sources of waste with examples

slides.narration: Namaste! Every kitchen, shop, factory and hospital throws something away. Some waste rots quickly, some lasts for centuries, and some is poisonous. If it is not collected and handled safely, it piles up, smells, pollutes and spreads disease. In this part we look at the harm caused by waste, why we must manage it, and five key environmental terms.

slides.heading: Spoilt landscapes and pollution
slides.body_md: **Spoilage of the landscape:** heaps of garbage along roads, railway tracks and riverbanks, and huge **dumping grounds** such as Ghazipur in Delhi and Deonar in Mumbai, which rise like hills and ruin the scenery. **Water pollution:** rainwater seeping through waste forms **leachate**, which carries chemicals into groundwater and streams; plastic bags **clog drains**, worsening urban floods. **Air pollution:** burning garbage gives off smoke and toxic gases; rotting waste releases **methane**, which can catch fire. **Soil pollution:** plastics, batteries and chemicals poison the soil.

visual.alt: Table of four harmful effects of waste and their causes

slides.narration: Uncollected waste spoils the look of our towns, from roadside heaps to dumps that rise like hills on the edge of big cities. Rain seeping through the rubbish forms a dirty liquid called leachate that poisons wells and streams. Plastic bags block drains, so streets flood. Burning garbage fills the air with smoke, and rotting waste gives off methane, which can catch fire.

slides.heading: Health hazards
slides.body_md: Garbage heaps are breeding grounds for **flies, mosquitoes and rats**, which spread **cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, dengue, malaria** and other diseases. Smoke from burning waste causes **breathing problems**. **Waste pickers** risk cuts, infections and poisoning from sharp, hazardous and biomedical waste. Stray **cattle** eat plastic bags and fall ill. After floods, rotting garbage and stagnant water raise the risk of epidemics — poor sanitation was one factor behind the plague outbreak in **Surat** in 1994.

rows: Waste pickers handling sharp or toxic waste

visual.alt: Table of health hazards caused by waste

slides.narration: Garbage heaps breed flies, mosquitoes and rats, which spread diseases such as cholera, typhoid, dengue and malaria. Smoke from burning rubbish harms the lungs. People who pick through waste for a living risk cuts, infections and poisoning. Even cattle suffer when they swallow plastic bags. After floods, rotting garbage can help epidemics break out, as happened in Surat in nineteen ninety four.

slides.heading: Quick check: impact of waste
slides.body_md: Link waste to a harmful effect.
slides.narration: Quick check. Leachate from dumps pollutes groundwater, and garbage heaps breed disease carriers.

slides.heading: Why waste management is essential
slides.body_md: **Growing cities produce more waste:** urban population and incomes are rising, and with them packaging and consumption. **Land is scarce:** cities are running out of space for dumps. **Public health:** proper collection and disposal prevent epidemics. **Clean environment:** protects rivers, groundwater, soil and air. **Resources:** waste contains valuable paper, metals, plastics and compost. **Jobs:** collection, recycling and composting employ many people. **Rules and missions:** the **Swachh Bharat Mission** (launched 2014) and the **Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016** require segregation at source (as of the early 2020s).

visual.alt: Table of reasons why waste management is needed

slides.narration: Indian cities are growing fast, and people are buying more packaged goods, so the amount of waste keeps rising while land for dumps runs out. Managing waste properly protects health and keeps rivers, wells and air clean. It also recovers valuable materials such as paper, metal and compost and gives work to many people. National missions and rules now require every home to separate its waste.

slides.heading: Worked example: trouble at a city dump
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A large open dump on the edge of a city has grown into a hill of garbage. Explain three ways in which it harms the people living nearby.

**Step 1. Water:** rain seeps through the waste and forms leachate, which pollutes wells and groundwater.

**Step 2. Air:** rotting waste releases methane; fires break out and fill the area with smoke and foul smells.

**Step 3. Health:** flies, mosquitoes and rats breed in the heap and spread disease; sometimes slopes of the heap collapse.

visual.alt: Flow showing how an open dump harms nearby residents through water, air and disease

slides.narration: An open dump harms its neighbours in three main ways. Rain soaks through the rubbish and carries poisons into wells as leachate. Rotting waste gives off methane, so fires break out and smoke and smells drift over homes. And flies, mosquitoes and rats breed in the heap and spread disease. Sometimes parts of a garbage hill even collapse.

slides.heading: Quick check: need for management
slides.body_md: Explain why cities must manage waste.
slides.narration: Quick check. More waste, scarce land and risks to health make waste management essential.

slides.heading: Global warming and acid rain
slides.body_md: **Global warming:** a rise in the average temperature of the Earth because **greenhouse gases** (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) trap heat. **Causes:** burning coal, oil and gas; deforestation; **methane from landfills**, flooded paddy fields and cattle. **Effects:** melting Himalayan glaciers, rising sea level threatening low coasts and islands such as the Sundarbans and Lakshadweep, more extreme heat waves and floods. **Acid rain:** rain made acidic when **sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides** from power stations, factories and vehicles mix with water vapour. **Effects:** corrodes buildings and monuments (marble yellows and pits), harms forests and crops, acidifies lakes and kills fish.

visual.alt: Table of a cause and an effect of global warming and acid rain

slides.narration: Global warming is the slow rise in the Earth’s average temperature as gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat. Burning fuels, cutting forests and rotting waste in landfills all add these gases. Glaciers melt and the sea rises. Acid rain forms when sulphur and nitrogen gases from chimneys and exhausts mix with rain. It eats into marble, harms forests and kills fish in lakes.

slides.heading: Eutrophication
slides.body_md: **Eutrophication** is the over-enrichment of a lake or slow river with **nutrients** — mainly **nitrates and phosphates** from fertiliser run-off, **untreated sewage** and detergents. The nutrients cause a rapid growth of **algae** (algal bloom) and water weeds. When they die, bacteria decompose them and use up the **dissolved oxygen**, so fish and other animals die and the water stinks. Urban lakes that receive sewage, such as Bellandur in Bengaluru, have suffered in this way.

visual.alt: Flow of eutrophication from nutrient inputs to algal bloom, decay, oxygen loss and fish death

slides.narration: Eutrophication happens when a lake receives too many nutrients, mostly nitrates and phosphates from farm fertilisers, sewage and detergents. Algae grow wildly and cover the water. When the algae die, bacteria break them down and use up the oxygen in the water, so fish suffocate and the lake begins to smell. Many city lakes that receive sewage have suffered this fate.

slides.heading: Thermal pollution
slides.body_md: **Thermal pollution** is the harmful rise in the temperature of a river, lake or sea when **hot water** from thermal or nuclear **power stations** and industries is discharged into it. Warm water holds **less dissolved oxygen**, speeds up the breathing of fish, kills sensitive species and eggs, and harms corals. **Remedies:** cool the water in **cooling towers** or **cooling ponds** before release, and reuse it in the plant.

rows: Hot water from power stations, industries
Less dissolved oxygen; fish and eggs die

visual.alt: Table of the cause, effect and remedy of thermal pollution

slides.narration: Power stations and factories use huge amounts of water for cooling and often release it back into rivers or the sea while it is still hot. This is thermal pollution. Warm water holds less oxygen, so fish struggle to breathe, and their eggs and young may die. The answer is to cool the water in cooling towers or ponds first, and reuse it.

slides.heading: Biomagnification
slides.body_md: **Biomagnification** is the increase in the concentration of a **persistent, non-biodegradable** poison (such as the pesticide DDT, or mercury and lead) at each **higher level of a food chain**. The poison is not broken down or excreted, so each animal stores what it eats; a predator eating many prey collects far more. **Cause:** pesticide run-off and industrial waste reaching water. **Effects:** birds of prey lay thin-shelled eggs that break; mercury in fish once poisoned people at Minamata in Japan.

slides.narration: Some poisons, such as certain pesticides and mercury, are never broken down. Tiny plants and animals in a lake absorb them, small fish eat many of those, large fish eat many small fish, and birds eat the large fish. At every step the poison becomes more concentrated. Top predators suffer most: birds of prey may lay thin shelled eggs, and people eating poisoned fish can fall ill.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading the food chain
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using the illustrative figures, (a) how many times more concentrated is the pesticide in the fish-eating bird than in the plankton? (b) Why does this happen?

**(a)** $\dfrac{10}{0.04} = 250$ times.

**(b)** The pesticide is persistent: it is not broken down or excreted, so it builds up in body fat. Each predator eats many prey and keeps the poison from all of them, so the concentration rises at each step.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative pesticide concentrations along a food chain

slides.narration: Divide the bird’s concentration by the plankton’s: the poison is two hundred and fifty times more concentrated in the bird. This happens because the pesticide is not broken down or passed out of the body. Every predator eats many prey and keeps all of their poison, so the amount stored keeps multiplying as we move up the food chain.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Accumulated waste spoils the landscape, pollutes water (leachate), air (burning, methane) and soil, and spreads disease.
Waste management is essential: more urban waste, scarce land, health, environment, resources, jobs; Swachh Bharat Mission and the 2016 rules.
Global warming: greenhouse gases trap heat; acid rain: sulphur and nitrogen oxides.
Eutrophication: excess nutrients → algal bloom → oxygen loss; thermal pollution: hot water discharge.
Biomagnification: persistent poisons concentrate up the food chain.

visual.alt: Summary table of five key terms and their causes

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Waste left to pile up spoils the landscape, poisons water, air and soil, and spreads disease, so growing cities must manage it. Global warming comes from heat trapping gases, acid rain from sulphur and nitrogen gases, eutrophication from too many nutrients, thermal pollution from hot water, and biomagnification from poisons that build up along food chains.

decks.title: Waste Management — Part 2: Safe disposal and the three Rs
goals: Explain why segregation at source is the first step of waste management
Suggest ways to reduce, reuse and recycle waste at home and school
Work out shares of household waste from illustrative data

slides.heading: From bin to benefit
slides.body_md: Part 2 — Safe disposal starts at home. Waste that is **separated** can be **composted**, **recycled** or **safely landfilled**; mixed waste can only be dumped. The best waste of all is the waste we never create — the idea behind **reduce, reuse, recycle**.

rows: Separates wet, dry and hazardous waste at home
Turns dry waste into new products

visual.alt: Table of methods of safe disposal and what each does

slides.narration: In this part we follow waste from the bin to safe disposal. If waste is separated at home, the wet part can become compost, the dry part can be recycled, and only a little needs to be buried in a properly built landfill. Mixed waste can only be dumped. Best of all is to create less waste in the first place, by reducing, reusing and recycling.

slides.heading: Segregation at source: the first step
slides.body_md: **Segregation at source** means separating waste where it is produced — in the home, school or shop — into: **wet (biodegradable)** waste such as food scraps and garden waste (**green bin**); **dry** waste such as paper, plastic, glass and metal (**blue bin**); and **domestic hazardous** waste such as batteries, broken bulbs, medicines and paint, kept separately. **Why first:** clean wet waste can be composted and clean dry waste recycled; hazardous items are kept away from people and soil; much less goes to landfill; waste workers are safer; collection is cheaper.

visual.alt: Flow of household waste separated into wet, dry and hazardous streams, each with its own destination

slides.narration: Segregation at source means sorting waste where it is made. Food scraps and garden waste go into the green bin, paper, plastic, glass and metal into the blue bin, and batteries, broken bulbs and old medicines are kept apart. This is the first step because clean wet waste can become compost and clean dry waste can be recycled, while dangerous items are kept away from people.

slides.heading: What is in a household bin?
slides.body_md: The chart shows the illustrative daily waste of one household: total 2.0 kg. **Wet** kitchen and garden waste is 50%; **recyclable** dry waste (paper, plastic, glass and metal) is 0.6 kg, or 30%; dust and inert material 15%; domestic hazardous waste 5%. Most of a typical Indian household’s waste is wet and can be composted.

slides.narration: This chart shows what one imaginary household throws away in a day: two kilograms in all. Half of it is wet kitchen and garden waste, which could be composted. Paper, plastic, glass and metal make up nearly a third and could be recycled. Only the dust, inert material and the small hazardous part really need special disposal.

slides.heading: Quick check: segregation
slides.body_md: Place an item in the correct bin.
slides.narration: Quick check. Food scraps go in the green bin; paper and plastic go in the blue bin.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much can a household divert?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using the household figures, find (a) the share of recyclable dry waste, (b) the waste produced in a week, and (c) the percentage of waste kept out of the dump if wet waste is composted and dry waste recycled.

**(a)** $\dfrac{0.6}{2.0} \times 100 = 30$%.

**(b)** $2.0 \times 7 = 14$ kg.

**(c)** $\dfrac{1.0 + 0.6}{2.0} \times 100 = 80$%.

visual.alt: Table of the household waste streams and destinations

slides.narration: The recyclable dry waste is six tenths of a kilogram out of two, which is thirty per cent. In a week the family throws away fourteen kilograms. If the wet waste is composted and the dry waste recycled, one point six kilograms a day never reach the dump, which is eighty per cent of the total. Segregation makes that possible.

slides.heading: Dumping: open dumps and sanitary landfills
slides.body_md: **Open dumping** — tipping mixed waste on open land or low-lying areas — is cheap but causes leachate, methane fires, smoke, smells, flies and rats, and wastes land. A **sanitary landfill** is an engineered site: a pit lined with **clay and plastic**, **leachate collected** and treated, waste spread in thin **cells** with **daily soil cover**, **gas vents** for methane, and a final **clay cap** with soil and grass. Under the 2016 rules, only **inert rejects** that cannot be composted or recycled should go to landfills. Problems: land near cities is scarce and costly, and landfills fill up.

visual.alt: Table comparing an open dump and a sanitary landfill

slides.narration: Open dumping simply tips mixed rubbish on open ground. It is cheap, but it pollutes groundwater, catches fire, smells and breeds disease. A sanitary landfill is carefully built: the pit is lined with clay and plastic, the leachate is piped away for treatment, each day’s waste is covered with soil, methane is vented, and the finished site is capped and grassed. Only waste that cannot be reused should go there.

slides.heading: Inside a sanitary landfill
slides.body_md: Follow the layers from the bottom: **groundwater** lies safely below a **clay and plastic liner**; a **leachate pipe** on the liner carries polluted liquid to treatment; waste is laid in **cells** separated by **daily soil cover**; a **vent** releases or collects **methane**; a **clay cap, soil and grass** seal the top when the landfill is full.

slides.heading: Composting and vermicomposting
slides.body_md: **Composting** is the decomposition of **biodegradable** waste by **microbes**, in the presence of **air**, into dark, crumbly, humus-rich **compost** (manure). In a **pit or bin**, kitchen waste is layered with dry leaves and a little soil, kept moist and turned regularly; it is ready in about six to eight weeks. In **vermicomposting**, **earthworms** eat the waste and leave nutrient-rich castings. Compost returns nutrients to the soil, cuts the need for chemical fertilisers and keeps wet waste out of dumps, where it would rot without air and give off methane.

Layer the scraps with dry leaves and a little soil, keep the heap moist and turn it now and then, and in six to eight weeks it is ready. Compost feeds the soil, saves fertiliser and keeps wet waste out of dumps, where it would rot and give off methane.

slides.heading: Worked example: landfill or compost?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A municipality must decide what to do with its wet waste. Compare dumping it in a landfill with composting it under four headings.

**Land:** landfill uses scarce land for decades; composting needs small yards or home pits.

**Pollution:** wet waste in landfills rots without air, producing methane and leachate; composting is aerobic and produces little methane.

**Product:** landfill gives nothing back; composting gives manure.

**Cost and care:** landfill needs transport and engineering; composting needs segregated waste and regular turning.

visual.alt: Table comparing landfill dumping with composting for wet waste

slides.narration: Compare the two for wet waste. A landfill eats up scarce land for decades, and buried food waste rots without air, giving off methane and leachate. Composting needs little space, produces little methane because air reaches the waste, and gives back useful manure. Its only demands are that waste be separated and that the heaps be kept moist and turned.

slides.heading: Reduce, reuse, recycle
slides.body_md: **Why:** natural resources and energy are saved; less waste reaches dumps; pollution falls; recycling gives jobs. **Reduce** (best): carry **cloth bags** and refillable bottles; refuse **single-use plastics** (India banned several such items from July 2022, as of the early 2020s); buy loose or in larger packs; plan meals to avoid food waste. **Reuse:** use glass jars and boxes again; write on both sides of paper; repair rather than replace; pass on books, uniforms and clothes. **Recycle:** give paper, cardboard, metal, glass and plastic to recyclers or the kabadiwala; send **e-waste** to authorised collectors.

rows: Book banks; both sides of paper

visual.alt: Table of ways to reduce, reuse and recycle at home and at school

slides.narration: The three Rs save resources and energy and cut pollution. Reducing is best: carry a cloth bag and a refillable bottle, refuse single use plastic and do not waste food. Reusing means giving things a second life: jars, boxes, paper used on both sides, and books and uniforms passed on. Recycling turns paper, metal, glass and plastic into new products.

slides.heading: Good practice in Indian cities and schools
slides.body_md: **Indore** became known for segregating waste into several streams and composting wet waste, and was ranked India’s cleanest city in several national surveys (as of the early 2020s). **Alappuzha** in Kerala manages much of its waste through home and community composting. In **Pune**, a cooperative of waste pickers (SWaCH) collects segregated waste door to door. Schools can run **compost pits**, **paper recycling drives**, **plastic-free campuses** and **e-waste collection boxes**.

slides.narration: Some Indian towns show what is possible. Indore separates its waste into several streams and composts the wet part, and it has repeatedly topped national cleanliness surveys. Alappuzha in Kerala composts much of its waste at home and in neighbourhoods. In Pune, a cooperative of waste pickers collects separated waste from homes. Your school can start with a compost pit and a paper drive.

Wet waste should be composted, dry waste recycled, hazardous waste collected separately, and only the leftovers placed in a properly built landfill. And the best way to manage waste is to make less of it, by reducing, reusing and recycling.

sections.heading: 1. Impact of waste accumulation
sections.body_md:
- **Spoilage of landscape:** roadside heaps; giant dumps such as Ghazipur (Delhi) and Deonar (Mumbai); littered riverbanks and beaches.
- **Pollution:** leachate pollutes groundwater and streams; plastic clogs drains and worsens floods; burning garbage and methane fires pollute air; plastics and chemicals poison soil.
- **Health hazards:** flies, mosquitoes and rats spread cholera, typhoid, dengue and malaria; smoke causes breathing problems; waste pickers face injury and infection; cattle eat plastic.

sections.heading: 2. Need for waste management
sections.body_md:
- Urban population, incomes and packaging are rising, so waste is increasing.
- Land for dumps near cities is scarce and costly.
- Protects public health and prevents epidemics.
- Protects water, soil and air.
- Recovers resources (compost, paper, metals, plastics) and creates jobs.
- Swachh Bharat Mission (2014) and the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 require segregation at source (as of the early 2020s).

sections.heading: 3. Key environmental terms
sections.body_md:
| Term | Meaning | One cause | One effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global warming | Rise in Earth’s average temperature as greenhouse gases trap heat | Burning fossil fuels; methane from landfills | Melting glaciers; rising sea level |
| Acid rain | Rain made acidic by sulphur and nitrogen oxides | Smoke from power stations, factories, vehicles | Corrodes marble monuments; kills fish in lakes |
| Eutrophication | Over-enrichment of water with nutrients | Fertiliser run-off, sewage, detergents | Algal bloom; oxygen loss; fish die |
| Biomagnification | Rise in concentration of persistent poisons up a food chain | DDT, mercury in water | Thin eggshells in birds of prey; poisoning |
| Thermal pollution | Harmful heating of water bodies | Hot water from power stations, industries | Less dissolved oxygen; fish die |

sections.heading: 4. Segregation and dumping
sections.body_md:
- **Segregation at source:** wet (biodegradable) — green bin; dry (paper, plastic, glass, metal) — blue bin; domestic hazardous (batteries, bulbs, medicines, paint) — separate.
- **Why first:** enables composting and recycling; isolates hazardous items; reduces landfill; protects waste workers; cheaper handling.
- **Open dumping:** cheap but causes leachate, methane fires, smell, flies, rats; wastes land.
- **Sanitary landfill:** clay and plastic liner; leachate collection and treatment; daily soil cover; gas vents; final clay cap with soil and grass; only inert rejects should go there.

key_terms.definition_md: Separating waste into wet, dry and hazardous kinds where it is produced.
An engineered, lined and covered site for the safe burial of waste that cannot be recovered.

sections.heading: 5. Composting
sections.body_md:
- **Composting:** aerobic decomposition of biodegradable waste by microbes into humus-rich manure; pit or bin; layers of kitchen waste, dry leaves and soil; kept moist and turned; ready in about six to eight weeks.
- **Vermicomposting:** earthworms eat the waste and produce nutrient-rich castings.
- **Landfill vs composting:** landfill uses large land for decades, produces methane and leachate, gives no product; composting needs little land, produces little methane, gives manure, but needs segregated waste and care.

Composting with the help of earthworms.

- **Reuse:** glass jars, both sides of paper, repair, pass on books and uniforms.

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) Separated wet waste can be composted and dry waste recycled, while hazardous items are kept away from people and soil; much less waste then needs disposal.

(d) Kitchen and garden waste is layered with dry leaves and soil in a pit or bin, kept moist and turned so that microbes (or earthworms) break it down with air into manure in six to eight weeks. Advantages: gives manure for soil; keeps wet waste out of landfills, reducing methane and leachate.

(b) They save natural resources and energy; they cut the waste reaching scarce landfills and so reduce pollution (also jobs).

(c) Refillable bottles and steel boxes with no single-use plastic; a compost pit for canteen and garden waste; a paper and e-waste collection drive with recyclers.

(d) Largely true: most household waste is wet or recyclable, so composting and recycling could divert most of it. answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Wet $= \dfrac{1.0}{2.0} \times 100 = 50$%; recyclable $= \dfrac{0.6}{2.0} \times 100 = 30$%.

(c) $50 + 30 = 80$%. The dust and inert material should go to a sanitary landfill and the domestic hazardous waste to a separate hazardous-waste collection.
